rv.q: Like the original Poltergeist films, this feels clunky and kitsch.
As it is, this first big opening of the year is a damp firework that splutters and goes phut.
All this could be both unsettling and intriguing and yet here it runs into the ground.
But sadly this limp effort will barely raise more than a sigh.
Was I bovvered? Not nearly enough.
It’s worse than that in a way: it’s a bore.
Yet why this sub-standard show is taking up a West End theatre is surely the greatest mystery of them all.
The whole cast conduct themselves with fortitude in Angus Jackson’s dingy, dog’s dinner of a production — booked to run until March 2 — that works neither as an investigation nor a spooker.
The most terrifying thing about ‘The Enfield Haunting’ is that nobody stepped in to stop it before it reached the West End.
Paul Unwin’s play, inspired by the notorious case of a poltergeist said to be rattling around a house in the London suburbs in the 1970s, is certain to make the list of worst plays of the year.
Angus Jackson’s production, despite the star casting of Catherine Tate and David Threlfall, is coarse, clumsy and so fright-free that it makes The Woman in Black look like The Exorcist.
They should have braced them against a feeble script and a production that quavers along as if afraid of its own ghost.
The Enfield Haunting manages to accurately portray the various nuances within the original hysteria that surrounded the allegations, while also delivering a fun, easy watch for an audience.

But the third time is not the charm for The Enfield Haunting, a bewildering muddle of a play from Paul Unwin that delayed its opening from one side of Christmas to the other and still poses far more questions than its 75 minutes are able to answer.
Unfortunately, this does not add up to a satisfactory play.

The storyline is impossible to follow because the basic set up isn’t properly explained and the knotty script is crowded with references to people such as ‘Mr Fairplay’ and ‘the Brazilians’ who don’t ever appear on stage.
Angus Jackson directs a sloppy script that goes nowhere.
The real mystery here is why The Enfield Haunting, directed by Angus Jackson, is so crushingly bad.
Angus Jackson’s insecure production is lacking in atmosphere.
...the show cannot be saved from its incoherent script and poor casting...This suggests a troubled production, that sadly is the true haunting at Theatre.

cn.t: A tedious misfire that wastes a crackling real-life story and talented cast. Critics found it flat, incoherent, and shockingly dull, with more unintentional laughs than scares—a mystery how such promising elements produced such lifeless results.
